title: A Child Left in the Night
subtitle: Vasudeva swaps Krishna for Yashoda's newborn daughter
story:
Two children had come into the world that night, in two households far apart. In the prison of Mathura, Devaki had borne a son — and Kamsa, the king of that city, had sworn that no child of hers would live. Among the cowherds of Vraja, Yashoda, the wife of Nanda, had borne a daughter. Before the night was over, the two children would change places, and neither of the two mothers would ever know it.

Vasudeva — Devaki's husband, and father of the newborn in his arms — walked into the sleeping settlement, the child wrapped against the dark. Only hours before, the boy had been born in the locked cell where his parents were kept. He moved quickly, the way a man moves when he knows the night will not last forever. Now the cowherd houses lay sunk in sleep: no one awake to see him pass, no lamp lit in any window. He came at last to Yashoda's house and stepped inside, where the household lay lost to the world and the only sound was the soft breathing of sleep.

There, in the stillness, he did the thing the whole night's journey had been for. He laid his son in Yashoda's bed, beside the sleeping mother. Then he took up the girl-child who lay there, the daughter born to Yashoda in that same night, and lifted her into his arms in his son's place. The exchange was made in silence: one child left behind, another carried away, while the house slept on and knew nothing of what had passed through it. It left no mark that anyone would ever find.

He carried the girl out into the dark and made his way back through the sleeping settlement, past the houses and the cattle yards, to the city and the prison and its locked rooms. There he laid her down beside Devaki, on the bed, in the very place where his own son had lain a few hours before. Then, quietly, he took up again the chains that held him, so that nothing would seem to have changed and the night would close over the whole thing as if it had never happened.

When Yashoda woke, she knew nothing of what the night had done. The child sleeping in her bed was not the one she had borne, and she would never be told. To her, simply and completely, the child was her son.

It was the one kindness the night allowed: that neither mother would wake to a loss she could name. And so the son of Vasudeva and Devaki grew up calling Yashoda mother, while the city, the prison, and the fear that had driven his father through the dark lay far behind him.
reflection: The force of the scene is in what no one knows: Yashoda does not realize what has been born to her, and the exchange succeeds precisely because it leaves no trace. The concealment that keeps the child safe is also, for the two mothers, a lifelong unknowing.
tradition_note: The Harivamsha identifies Yashoda's daughter as the goddess of sleep, born of a portion of Vishnu's energy; the Bhagavata narrates only the exchange itself.
next_story_tease: By morning, the cowherd settlement would throw itself into celebration of the child who had arrived in the night.
hero_scene: Vasudeva in the dim light of Yashoda's sleeping house, setting his newborn son down in her bed and lifting her daughter into his arms, the two children exchanged in silence while the household sleeps on.
